common_name: Regent Japanese Pagoda Tree (Regent Scholar Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped grafted trees in well-drained, adaptable, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Regent' was selected by the U.S. National Arboretum for its faster growth rate, straighter trunk, and more uniform oval crown than seed-grown trees, and it begins flowering at 8-10 years of age rather than the 10-20+ years typical of seedlings.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, adaptable, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; 'Regent' is the most widely planted named cultivar of Japanese pagoda tree, selected for a faster growth rate, straighter central leader, and denser, more symmetrical oval-to-rounded crown than seed-grown trees. Like the species it produces large panicles of creamy-white, pea-like flowers in mid to late summer that are a major nectar source for honeybees, followed by ornamental bright-green bead-like seed pods that persist into winter. Its principal advantage over seedling trees is precocity: 'Regent' begins flowering reliably within 8-10 years of planting, compared with 10-20 years or more for seed-grown specimens, making it the preferred choice for street tree and urban shade tree plantings where a predictable, uniform habit and earlier bloom are valued. Tolerant of heat, drought, compacted soil, and urban pollution once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; 'White Robin' is the white-flowered selection of ragged robin and, like the species, is an obligate of consistently moist to wet soils.

directions: Plant divisions in moist to wet, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; 'White Robin' is a pure-white-flowered selection of ragged robin, producing the same deeply and narrowly cut, feathery, four-lobed petals as the wild rose-pink to magenta form but in clean white on slender, branching stems in early summer. Like the species it requires consistently moist to wet soil and is best suited to wet meadow, bog garden, and pond-margin plantings, where its pale flowers show up beautifully against darker foliage and standing water. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor; because seedlings can revert toward the species' pink coloring, division rather than seed is the reliable way to keep the true white form.

planting.note: Direct-sow seeds on the soil surface in early spring or fall in well-drained, lean to moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; seeds need light and should not be covered. 'Canon Went' comes fairly true from seed when grown in isolation from the purple-flowered species.

directions: Scatter seeds on bare, well-drained, lean soil in full sun in early spring or fall, pressing lightly onto the surface without covering; 'Canon Went' is a soft, dusky-pink-flowered sport of purple toadflax, bearing the same slender, airy spikes of tiny snapdragon-like flowers as the species but in a warm shell-pink rather than lavender-purple, over the same delicate blue-green, needle-like foliage. It blooms from late spring through midsummer and intermittently afterward, and shares the species' exceptional drought tolerance and preference for dry, stony, or poor alkaline soils, where it self-seeds and naturalizes in gravel gardens, dry banks, and old walls. Cutting back spent stems encourages repeat flowering through autumn; allow some seed to scatter each year to maintain the pink-flowered colony, though a percentage of purple-flowered seedlings may appear over time.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before last frost; soak seeds for 12-24 hours before sowing; plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. 'QIS Orange' is part of the QIS (Quality Improved Strain) series bred for long, strong stems suited to commercial cut-flower production.

directions: Start seeds indoors 4-6 weeks before transplanting (soaking seeds first improves germination); plant in well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. 'QIS Orange' is a member of the QIS (Quality Improved Strain) series of Haage globe amaranth, bred for taller, longer, and stronger stems than open-pollinated strains, producing clover-like, papery, rounded flower heads about 1-1.5 inches across in vivid golden-orange on plants well-suited to professional cut-flower production as well as home gardens. The papery flower heads hold their color perfectly when air-dried, making them outstanding everlastings for dried arrangements. Heat and drought tolerance is exceptional, with plants blooming prolifically through humid summers without mildew or decline; deadheading is unnecessary, as flowering continues over a very long season until frost. Butterflies visit the flower heads frequently, and the long, straight stems make this selection a favorite among cut-flower growers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Annual Flowers

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, moderately fertile, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade in spring; 'Plenum Violaceum' is a fully double, sterile-flowered form that must be propagated by division rather than seed.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, moderately fertile, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; 'Plenum Violaceum' is an old, fully double-flowered form of meadow cranesbill, its violet-blue flowers packed with extra petals into rounded rosettes rather than the simple open cup of the species. Because the flowers are sterile and produce no seed, individual blooms last considerably longer than those of single-flowered forms, and the plant channels no energy into seed production, often resulting in a longer and more generous bloom period from early to midsummer. Like the species it forms large, robust clumps of deeply cut foliage and benefits from staking in exposed sites; cutting the plant back hard after flowering encourages fresh foliage and, in good conditions, a light second flush of bloom. As a sterile double it must be increased by division of established clumps rather than by seed, and named divisions are the only reliable way to obtain true stock.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown specimens in moist to moderately dry, slightly acidic to neutral, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun in spring; 'Golden Arrow' is grown for its gold-variegated foliage, which colors best with some direct sun but can scorch in hot, dry afternoon exposure.

directions: Plant divisions in moist to moderately dry, average to fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Golden Arrow' is a gold-variegated-leaved selection of mountain fleece, its heart-shaped leaves splashed and margined in creamy yellow-gold, giving the clump a bright, luminous presence in the border even before the flowers open. From summer into autumn it produces the same small, upright, bottle-brush spikes of rosy-red flowers typical of the species, which read as an attractive contrast against the pale foliage. Best foliage color develops with a few hours of direct sun, but plants appreciate afternoon shade in hot climates to prevent leaf scorch. Like other mountain fleece cultivars it forms a well-behaved, non-spreading clump and tolerates a wide range of moisture levels once established; divide congested clumps in spring to maintain vigorous, brightly variegated new growth.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in moist, moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade in spring; 'George Davidson' is a classic golden-yellow-flowered Crocosmia cultivar that, like the species, spreads by cormlets and forms expanding clumps over time.

directions: Plant corms in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; 'George Davidson' is a long-established Crocosmia cultivar bearing arching, branched sprays of clear golden-yellow, funnel-shaped flowers in mid to late summer above fans of pleated, sword-shaped, bright green leaves. It is one of the most reliably hardy and vigorous of the yellow-flowered Crocosmia cultivars, forming expanding clumps that are somewhat less aggressive than the wild species but still benefit from occasional division to maintain flowering vigor. The tubular flowers are highly attractive to hummingbirds and make excellent, long-lasting cut flowers. In zones 6-7, mulch corms heavily for winter or lift and store them frost-free like gladiolus; in zones 8-9 they can remain in the ground year-round. Excellent paired with the red-flowered 'Lucifer' for a two-tone late-summer display.

common_name: Rosea Flore Pleno Double Pink Hawthorn (Double Pink May)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container stock in spring or fall in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral, clay to loamy soil in full sun to part shade; 'Rosea Flore Pleno' is grown for its fully double, rose-pink May flowers and sets little to no fruit compared with single-flowered forms.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained to moderately moist, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to part shade; 'Rosea Flore Pleno' is one of the most popular ornamental flowering forms of midland hawthorn, smothering itself each May in fully double, rich rose-pink flowers carried in dense clusters along the branches — a striking contrast to the simple white or pale pink single flowers of the wild species. Because the flowers are double, they produce little or no fruit, so the tree's ornamental value rests entirely on its spectacular spring bloom and, secondarily, on its dense, twiggy, thorny branching habit, which still provides good nesting cover and winter structure for birds. It shares the species' tolerance of heavier clay soils and partial shade, and makes an excellent flowering specimen, hedgerow, or small ornamental tree in gardens too small for larger flowering trees. Being a grafted named clone, it must be propagated vegetatively to preserve its double flower form, as seedlings will revert to single flowers.

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; 'Pendula' is typically top-grafted onto an upright understock at a chosen height, and its ultimate size and form depend heavily on the height of the graft and how the leader is trained.

directions: Plant grafted trees in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, deep, moist to average, loamy or sandy soil in full sun; 'Pendula' is a strikingly weeping cultivar of European larch, its slender branches cascading straight downward from the point of grafting to form a curtain-like, sinuous curtain of soft, light-green needles that turn the same brilliant gold as the species each October. Because it is propagated by grafting an unstable weeping mutation onto upright rootstock, its ultimate shape depends on training: left untrained and grafted low, it forms a low, spreading mound; staked and grown as a standard, it makes a dramatic cascading specimen with a defined trunk and a curtain of pendulous branches, sometimes trained over an arbor or against a wall. It shares the species' fast growth, tolerance of cold and wind, and preference for full sun and well-drained soil, and is among the most popular and widely available weeping conifers for use as a singular accent specimen in both large and small gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock or divisions in spring in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Guizhou' is a dark-purple-flushed selection collected in Guizhou Province, China, that requires the same consistent moisture as the species.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in moist, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade to full sun; 'Guizhou' is a striking dark-foliaged selection of white mugwort, its stems and deeply divided leaves flushed a rich purple-black that deepens with sun exposure and contrasts dramatically with the tall, late-summer panicles of creamy-white, astilbe-like flower plumes held well above the foliage. Like the species, it is exceptional among artemisias for tolerating partial shade and requiring consistently moist soil rather than the dry, lean conditions most artemisias prefer, making it a valuable dark-foliage accent for shaded and part-shaded mixed borders where silver-leaved artemisias would fail. It is not invasive like many running artemisia species, forms a well-behaved clump, and benefits from staking in windy sites and from division every few years to maintain vigorous, deeply colored new growth. The flower plumes are excellent for cutting.
